drivingQuestion: What does the mishna mean by its three uncertainties?
outcomeNote: The mishna is read as an escalating progression.

segments.he: לָא מִיבַּעְיָא קָאָמַר: לָא מִיבַּעְיָא סָפֵק הוּא שָׁם סָפֵק אֵינוֹ שָׁם, דְּאִי אִיתֵיהּ חַי — הוּא דִּמְפַקְּחִין, אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ סָפֵק חַי סָפֵק מֵת — מְפַקְּחִין. וְלָא מִיבַּעְיָא סָפֵק חַי סָפֵק מֵת, דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ סָפֵק גּוֹי סָפֵק יִשְׂרָאֵל — מְפַקְּחִין.
segments.en: The Gemara explains: «It is speaking» using the style of: «Needless to say,» and the mishna should be understood as follows: «Needless to say,» in a case where it is «uncertain» whether «he is there or not there,» one removes the debris, since «if he is» there and he is «alive, one» must «clear» the debris. «But even» if it is «uncertain» whether he is «alive or dead, one» must «clear» the debris. «And needless to say,» when there is «uncertainty» whether he is «alive or dead,» but it is certain that he is «a Jew,» one must clear the debris. «Rather,» one must «clear» the debris «even if» there is «uncertainty» whether «he is a gentile or a Jew.»

moves.summary: the mishna escalates: not only... but even

edges.about: the mishna uses 'needless to say' form: each uncertainty is a further stage
answers what the mishna means by its three uncertainties

positions.claim: one clears debris even when uncertain whether the victim is a gentile or Jew
